newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand's central bank loosens monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand's central bank loosens monetary policy.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash, known for his "hands-off" approach to monetary policy, on Friday endorsed an easing of monetary conditions.
Brash sanctioned a one percentage point easing in monetary conditions in his biannual Monetary Policy Statement (MPS), a move supported by the country's low inflation environment.
"The Reserve Bank is increasingly confident that inflation pressures are dropping away, and for the second time in six months we are able to ease monetary policy," Brash said.
"However, actual monetary conditions have already eased considerably, fully anticipating today's statement, and we are not seeking a further easing in conditions," he told reporters.
Brash said, provided the economy panned out as forecast, another easing of 40 basis points was likely in the December quarter.

But that margin was immediately factored in by financial markets, which had already loosened monetary conditions recently in anticipation of a sluggish economy and an easier stance from the central bank.
New Zealand financial markets have been in monetary easing mode for the last six months as policy makers attempted to coax the stalled economy back to life.
The postponement of tax cuts, uncertainty surrounding the formation of the new government late last year and cyclical factors had resulted in a faster-than-expected economic slowdown.
"The bank now believes that the economy grew more slowly in the first two quarters of 1997 than we thought likely when we issued our March Economic Projections," Brash said.
The central bank predicted a sharp upturn in the economy from mid-1998 as a big fiscal stimulus and planned tax cuts in 1998 kicked in.
The bank has forecast a 2.0 percent growth rate for the year to March 1998, compared with a Treasury forecast of 2.4 percent. Treasury's forecast was revised down from an earlier 3.6 percent.

The central bank's growth forecasts were more conservative than Treasury forecasts in Thursday's government budget. The bank expected annual growth at 3.6 percent in the year to March 1999, rising to 3.8 percent in the year to March 2000.
Treasury's prediction for growth in the year to March 1999 stands at 4.2 percent, but falls to 3.5 percent in the year to March 2000.
The bank on Thursday introduced a new monetary conditions index as a tool to monitor and influence monetary conditions but will continue to allow financial markets set the pace.
Brash defended the "hands-off" approach, including the bank's decision this month not to adopt an official cash rate used by most central banks to control monetary conditions.
"The main reason for that I think is that in New Zealand interest rates and the exchange rate have an effect on inflation, both in the short term and the medium term," he said.
"We felt that by moving to an interest rate target only, we might move the market's attention from the total effect of monetary conditions -- both interest rates and the exchange rate."
Australian Treasury Secretary Ted Evans has said New Zealand's focus on inflation was too narrow, causing balance of payments problems and an over-inflated exchange rate.
But Brash said that New Zealand's record of growth and employment in the 1990s stood up well, comparatively.
"At the trough of our cycle we are seeing growth only slightly lower than what we estimate the economy's sustainable long-term growth rate is. We expect it to accelerate that growth rate next year."
"There is nothing in our employment numbers, nothing in our growth numbers that would lead me to agree with Mr Evans on that point," Brash said.
The central bank has forecast the underlying inflation rate to halve to one percent next year and stabilise there until nearly 2000.
